issues.legal_issue: In a landlord’s suit for possession, the term “decree” refers to the decree finally disposing of the suit, including an appellate decree where a competent appeal is pending.
material_facts: A trial court decreed a landlord’s suit for possession against a tenant.
The tenant filed a competent appeal, which remained pending when a statutory restriction on eviction became applicable to the premises.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could invoke the statutory protection during the appeal; the relevant decree was the decree finally disposing of the suit, and the appellate decree governed.
issues.legal_principle: An appeal is a continuation of the suit. When an appellate decree affirms, modifies, or reverses the trial decree on the merits, the trial decree merges into the appellate decree. The Court relied on the principles in Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subhash Chandra Yograj Sinha and Mst. Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Cheetri.

predicates.tenant_possession_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession of premises from a tenant.
predicates.competent_appeal_pending: The tenant filed a competent appeal against the trial court’s decree, and that appeal remained pending.

issues.definition: When a landlord’s possession suit is under a competent appeal, the tenant may invoke applicable protection before the appellate court finally disposes of the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A change in tenancy law that takes effect while an appeal in a possession suit is pending governs the parties’ rights in that appeal, even if the suit was filed before the change took effect.
material_facts: The landlord filed a suit for possession before the statutory protection applied to the premises.
The protection became applicable during the tenant’s pending first appeal and restricted possession decrees to specified grounds.
The eviction ground relied on was not among the statutory exceptions, and the landlord’s notice did not meet the statutory notice requirement.
issues.conclusion: The changed law governed the pending appeal. Because no applicable exception displaced the protection and the required notice had not been given, the suit was incompetent and was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory restriction on making a possession order protects a tenant by limiting the court’s power to make an effective order or decree, and applies to pending matters where its language and purpose so require. A change in law during an appeal governs the parties’ rights because an appeal is a continuation or rehearing of the suit. The Court applied sections 13(1) and 13(6) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, and relied on Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subhash Chandra Yograj Sinha, Mst. Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Cheetri, Ram Sarup v. Munshi, Mula v. Godhu, Amarjit Kaur v. Pritam Singh, and the principles discussed in Dayawati v. Inderjit, Kristnama Chariar v. Mangammal, and Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri.

rule.if: tenant_possession_appeal and suit_preceded_protection and protection_became_applicable_during_appeal and asserted_ground_outside_exceptions and required_notice_not_given

predicates.tenant_possession_appeal: A landlord’s suit seeking possession from a tenant was under appeal.
predicates.suit_preceded_protection: The landlord filed the possession suit before the protective tenancy law became applicable to the premises.
predicates.protection_became_applicable_during_appe: A law restricting possession orders became applicable to the premises while the appeal was pending.
predicates.asserted_ground_outside_exceptions: The landlord relied on a ground that was not within an exception to the law’s restriction on possession orders.
predicates.required_notice_not_given: The landlord did not give the tenant the notice required before filing the possession suit.

issues.definition: If a possession suit filed before a protective law applies is under appeal when the law becomes applicable, and the relied-on ground is not excepted and the required notice was not given, the suit is incompetent.
